title: Greedy Best-First in Chicago: Fast Rush or Trap? ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First Search pick the next “closest-looking” block using a heuristic and advance toward the goal. In this Chicago (Loop) map, you’ll see exactly why it can look brilliant fast—and still fail compared to Greedy vs A* behavior.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — why does it rush to the goal ⚡ and when does it fail?

In the video: each grid intersection becomes a node, edges connect drivable blocks, and Greedy Best-First always expands the frontier node with the lowest heuristic h(n) (typically straight-line distance to the target).

Deep technical breakdown:
• Greedy Best-First uses ONLY h(n), not the full cost-so-far g(n).
• So it can “look” efficient locally, but miss cheaper routes that require moving away from the goal.
• That’s the failure mode: misleading heuristics + obstacles create deceptive shortcuts.

Takeaway: Greedy Best-First is fast and goal-directed, but it’s not guaranteed optimal—A* accounts for g(n) too.

Debate question: Should a robot prioritize “closest now” (Greedy) or “cheapest overall” (A*) when the map is cluttered?

Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison in Chicago (Loop) 🇺🇸 ⚡

In this Shorts visualization, we implement heuristic pathfinding using Greedy Best-First: it always expands the frontier with the smallest h(n) (distance-to-go). Watch where it rushes toward the destination—and when obstacles + deceptive heuristics cause it to miss the optimal route.

You’ll learn:
• greedy best first search mechanics (h(n) only)
• why greedy vs a star differs (no g(n) vs g(n)+h(n))
• when heuristic pathfinding breaks down
